fetched_contents.text: Predicting the effect of residual stress on fatigue crack growth Abstract Fatigue crack growth from a hole with a pre-existing compressive residual stress is simulated using two-dimensional elastic–plastic finite element analyses. The analyses allow a determination of the crack opening stress as the crack propagates through the residual stress, from which the effective stress intensity factor range ΔKeff and the fatigue crack growth is predicted. Results from these simulations are compared with experimental data and to predictions made using a conventional superposition of the elastic stress intensity factor. The crack closure-based methodology resulted in predictions which compared well with the experimental data, while the results using superposition were nonconservative. Predictions from the closure-based method are highly dependent on the da/dN = f(ΔKeff) constitutive relationship used, highlighting the need for experimental methods to reliably measure this correlation. Introduction The effect of residual stress on fatigue crack propagation is of great practical significance and has been the focus of much research. This research has been reviewed in several studies [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. Superposition techniques are often used when assessing the effects of a known residual stress field on fatigue crack propagation. The superposition involves the computation of a stress intensity factor (K)R which is associated with the initial pre-existing residual stress field. This factor it then superposed upon the stress intensity factor that results from external loading (K)L to give the total resultant stress intensity factor for the maximum and minimum loads:Kmax=(Kmax)L+(K)RKmin=(Kmin)L+(K)RThe stress intensity factor range and stress ratio is then calculated:ΔK=Kmax-Kmin=(Kmax)L-(Kmin)LR=KminKmaxThe stress intensity factor range ΔK is independent of the residual stress, and only the stress ratio R is affected. Fatigue crack growth is then predicted using a correlation of the form:dadN=f(ΔK,R)An alternate superposition-based methodology is also often employed [1], [2], [5]. In this alternate approach maximum and minimum values of the total resultant stress intensity factor K are computed for the cyclic loading (Eqs. (1), (2)), and negative resultant K values are set to zero to simulate a closed crack. A total resultant stress intensity factor range ΔK is then calculated. This resultant stress intensity factor range may then be used to compute the predicted fatigue crack growth rate da/dN in the residual stress field using a correlation of the form:dadN=f(ΔK,0)If fatigue crack growth is instead assumed to be a function of the form:dadN=f(ΔK,Kmax)such as that suggested by Vasudevan et al. [7], [8], then the value of Kmax would be computed using Eq. (1). Superposition-based techniques are used extensively because of their simplicity. The use of superposition has been criticized by some researchers because it considers only the initial residual stress field that exists in the uncracked structure, with no acknowledgement of the redistribution of residual stress that occurs as the propagating fatigue crack penetrates the residual stress field with its free or partially free surfaces [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. Other researchers have argued that the redistribution of residual stress is of no consequence [2], [16]. The redistribution of residual stress due to the presence of a crack at the surface of a cold-worked hole has been investigated numerically by Pavier et al. [17]. Bueckner [18] has demonstrated mathematically that, for linear elastic materials, stress intensity factors resulting from a given applied loading may be computed using the stress distribution in the uncracked structure. Heaton [19] has presented a mathematically rigorous proof that generalizes Bueckner’s formulation to include both thermal and pre-existing residual stress fields. The work of Bueckner and Heaton suggests that, for linear elastic materials, the redistribution of applied and residual stresses due to fatigue crack propagation is of no consequence when computing stress intensity factors and subsequent fatigue crack growth through use of Eq. (5), (6). The conclusions arrived by Bueckner and Heaton are applicable to linear elastic materials only. The existence of plastic deformation at the crack tip, even under small-scale yielding conditions, will produce crack-generated residual stresses at the crack tip [20], [21] and closure along the surface of the propagating crack [22], [23]. The superposition methodology is unable to account for the influence of these effects. Consequently, the use of linear elastic superposition techniques for prediction of the effects of residual stress on fatigue crack propagation may result in crack growth predictions that correlate poorly with experimental observations [1]. As an alternative to superposition-based fatigue crack growth prediction, the effective stress intensity factor range ΔKeff first introduced by Elber can be used [22], [23]. The effective stress intensity factor range is employed to enable consideration of crack closure in fatigue crack growth predictions. Elber considers that as a crack propagates, crack closure occurs as a result of plastically deformed material left in the path taken by the crack. This material is referred to as the plastic wake. The plastic wake enables the crack to close before minimum load is reached, and Elber reasoned that the stress intensity factor at the crack tip does not change while the crack is closed even when the applied load is changing. fetched_contents.text: Fatigue strength prediction in incrementally formed sheet-parts with varying residual stresses 1. Introduction Sheet metal forming is a key manufacturing discipline in automotive, aerospace, and construction engineering [1]. Without knowledge of material properties and material behavior under uniaxial, biaxial, or multiaxial [1,2] load, modern and innovative part design is not possible in those industries. While many sheet metal parts from the exterior of the automotive or transport industry are not exposed to cyclic loading [1], several components undergo cyclic loading during their lifetime [3,4]. Cyclic loading leads to premature failure of the component, often occurring at stress levels significantly lower than the material's yield strength [5,6]. That is why fatigue strength is a crucial mechanical property relevant to the use of metals and their alloys. In the high-cycle regime, where the applied macroscopic stresses are small and the induced plastic strain is negligible, the tensile strength, in particular, primarily determines the resistance against crack initiation as well as the compressive residual stresses and therefore the fatigue life [7]. A high tensile strength leads to an impeded dislocation movement, resulting in more cycles, or rather a longer time-period needed for crack initiation by the accumulation of microplastic deformations [8,9]. Besides the tensile strength, residual stresses are also an important influencing factor for fatigue strength [10,11]. Several studies show a beneficial influence of compressive residual stresses on fatigue behavior [12,13], whereas tensile residual stresses promote premature crack initiation and failure. Often, an additional processing step for the component is performed, either for relaxation of a detrimental residual stress state done by a heat treatment, or otherwise to induce beneficial compressive residual stresses in the component surface, for example, by mechanical or laser shot peening [14]. Additional process steps can be avoided (and resources can be saved) if a forming process is applied that already introduces large amounts of compressive residual stress. Among other processes, such as rolling [15] and deep drawing [16], incremental sheet forming (ISF) processes are very promising regarding the production of near-net-shaped components with distinct compressive residual stresses [[17], [18], [19]]. Especially, if a high formability is required, ISF processes are relevant [20]. For instance, in single point incremental forming (SPIF), the processing of high-strength materials and complex components can be achieved as a result of stress superposition in locally deformed areas [20]. It is possible to produce complex parts without the need for partial or solid dies, making SPIF one of the most flexible incremental sheet metal forming processes. Due to low tooling costs and high flexibility, SPIF is particularly suitable for small batch sizes and rapid prototyping [17]. Due to the localized deformation zone, very high strains occur locally, and a higher formability compared to conventional forming processes can be achieved [18]. Several recent studies were dealing with the characterization of residual stress during SPIF and with its modeling [[20], [21], [22], [23]]. For predicting material failure and damage, typically forming limit curves (FLC) and fracture forming limit lines are considered [24]. Predicting the lifetime of sheet metal forming processes involves an understanding of the complex interactions between material properties, forming techniques, and potential defects. Various models and methodologies have been developed to predict the durability and quality of formed sheet metal components [25,26]. These models incorporate factors such as fatigue behavior, forming-induced defects, and material failure, utilizing both experimental and simulation-based approaches. Real-time prediction of forming defects such as cracks and wrinkles can be achieved using machine learning models like Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and Artificial Neural Networks [[27], [28], [29]]. A review about the accurate integration of predicted residual stresses into fatigue-life calculations is essential for realistic predictions, as given in Ref. [30]. Another approach is the combination of FE simulation and subsequent fatigue analysis in commercial software, e.g. FE-Safe, where experimental data can also be used as input parameters [[31], [32], [33]]. In this study, a numerical approach based on FE-Safe software to predict the fatigue lifetime and crack initiation of SPIF-formed truncated cones made from aluminum alloy 5083 sheets is presented. The prediction is based on numerically determined residual stresses created in the SPIF process. This numerical model is validated with XRD measurements. Experimental fatigue testing of the SPIF material formed using different step-down increments in the process are performed to fit S–N curves as input parameters for FE-Safe simulations. As a further outcome, the iterative fitted S–N curve for one specific step-down increment value delivered very accurate results for the other step-down increments. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Residual stresses influence fatigue strength and failure behavior by altering the fatigue limit, changing the S–N curve shape, and affecting crack initiation and propagation. The evidence here shows that compressive residual stress improves fatigue life and that its effect on fatigue behavior can outperform surface roughness [N2-R1]. A study on incrementally formed sheet parts explicitly states that fatigue strength is crucial for metals and their alloys, and that compressive residual stresses and high tensile strength together determine resistance against crack initiation and fatigue life [N2-F2]. In the same context, it says that residual stresses are an important influencing factor for fatigue strength and that beneficial compressive residual stresses delay failure, while tensile residual stresses promote premature crack initiation and failure [N2-F2].

On the S–N curve shape, the key point is that residual stresses shift the relationship between alternating stress magnitude and cycles to failure. The case study on SPIF-formed truncated cones notes that fatigue lifetime and crack initiation were predicted using S–N curves fitted from experimental fatigue testing, and that residual stresses created in the forming process were numerically determined and validated with XRD measurements [N2-F2]. This implies that residual stress state can shift the curve upward or change its slope, depending on whether residual stresses are compressive or tensile. The broader fatigue literature also shows that the fatigue limit is affected by residual stresses and surface roughness, with higher compressive residual stress inducing longer fatigue life [N2-R1].

Residual stress redistribution affects crack initiation and propagation, but the evidence here is indirect. The SPIF case study shows that localized deformation introduces high strains and residual stresses, and that fatigue analysis must incorporate the residual stress field created by forming [N2-F2]. The fatigue crack propagation literature in the N1 evidence describes superposition methods for assessing residual stress effects, and notes that the redistribution of residual stress due to crack propagation is a major limitation of linear elastic superposition techniques [N1-F1]. That is, crack growth can change the residual stress field at the surface, making simple superposition insufficient for accurate predictions. The same source also says that crack closure and plastic wake effects are important in fatigue crack propagation, suggesting that residual stress redistribution is not just a passive background effect but a dynamic part of crack behavior [N1-F1].

Surface treatments like shot peening improve fatigue strength by generating beneficial compressive residual stresses. The shot-peening literature in N3 says shot peening is an efficient technique to improve fatigue behavior of metal components, and that each shot strike creates a dimple and beneficial compressive residual stress [N3-R2]. It also states that shot peening can have potentially positive effects on residual compressive stress, work hardening, surface roughness, and other factors [N3-R3]. The MDPI article further notes that shot peening can introduce residual compressive stresses on the surface of the part, which is especially relevant because most fatigue cracks in engineering practice occur from the surface [N6-R4]. The practical example in N6 also mentions that shot-peening residual stresses may have a detrimental effect in some cases if the largest defects are present, showing that the benefit depends on the local defect state [N6-R1]. Overall, shot peening improves fatigue strength by modifying the surface residual stress field, but its effectiveness is not absolute and depends on the part’s geometry, defect distribution, and loading conditions [N3-R2][N6-R1].

In short, residual stresses alter fatigue strength by shifting the fatigue limit upward when compressive, changing the S–N curve shape by modifying the stress–life relationship, and affecting failure behavior by delaying crack initiation and changing crack propagation paths. Surface treatments such as shot peening are used to improve fatigue strength by inducing favorable compressive residual stresses, but their effectiveness is limited by local defects and the interaction with external cyclic loading [N2-R1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N6-R1].

Residual stresses interact with external cyclic stresses in a way that is not simply additive; instead, they can modify the total stress state at the surface and influence crack behavior. The evidence from N1 shows that superposition techniques are commonly used to assess residual stress effects on fatigue crack propagation, but that these methods assume an initial residual stress field and do not account for redistribution as the crack propagates [N1-F1]. This means that residual stresses do not merely “add” to external cyclic stresses in a linear sense; they can be modified by crack growth and local plasticity, which changes how they combine with the applied load [N1-F1]. The same source also describes stress state parameters such as mean stress and load ratio as important because the stress intensity factor range ΔK is independent of residual stress, while the stress ratio R is affected [N1-F1].

Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and affect crack propagation by reducing the effective stress intensity range available for crack growth. The N1 evidence explicitly says that compressive residual stress can counterbalance elastic stress concentrations generated by features such as FOD notches when external cyclic load is applied [N1-R2]. It also states that crack closure-based methodology gives better predictions than conventional superposition, because crack closure reduces the effective ΔKeff and thus the crack growth rate [N1-F1]. The SPIF case study in N2 further supports this by showing that residual stresses are important for fatigue strength and that compressive residual stresses improve fatigue behavior [N2-F2]. Together, these sources suggest that compressive residual stresses do not simply subtract from the external load; they change the stress state in a way that delays crack initiation and reduces the effective driving force for crack propagation [N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-F2].

The role of stress state parameters such as mean stress and load ratio is central because the fatigue crack growth response depends on the combination of ΔK and R. The N1 source explains that fatigue crack growth is predicted using da/dN = f(ΔK, R), and that superposition methods are criticized for ignoring redistribution of residual stress and crack-generated residual stress [N1-F1]. The mean stress correction literature in N4 adds that mean stress correction is used to account for non-zero mean stresses and that the effect depends on material, stress state, environment, and strain amplitude [N4-R2]. This is important because the same external cyclic stress can behave differently depending on whether it is tensile mean, compressive mean, or zero mean, and the load ratio R controls how much of the cycle is spent at high stress versus low stress. In other words, residual stresses and external cyclic stresses jointly determine the effective stress state, and the stress ratio R is especially important for fatigue prediction because ΔK is independent of residual stress while R is not [N1-F1][N4-R2].

In summary, residual stresses do not simply add, subtract, or modify external cyclic stresses in a fixed way; instead, they interact by changing the local stress state and influencing crack closure, crack initiation, and crack propagation. Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and reduce crack propagation by counteracting elastic stress concentrations and increasing closure, while the stress state parameters mean stress and load ratio determine how the combined stress field affects fatigue life [N1-R2][N1-F1][N4-R2].

Residual stresses are measured using several common methods, each with distinct strengths and limitations. The N5 evidence identifies X-ray diffraction (XRD) and neutron diffraction as key methods. XRD is described as a nondestructive method for measuring residual stress in fine-grained crystalline materials, with surface measurements and subsurface measurement possible using line broadening and layer removal [N5-F3]. Neutron diffraction is noted as a specialized technique for bulk residual stress data in thick sections and as a complementary method to XRD for comparing results in welds and other structures [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The same source also mentions synchrotron diffraction as a method that can measure residual stresses at arbitrary depth, improving spatial resolution beyond conventional laboratory XRD [N5-R5].

A major limitation of XRD and related methods is that they depend on assumptions about the residual stress field, sample geometry, and linear elasticity. The N5 evidence states that mechanical methods are necessarily destructive and cannot be directly checked by repeat measurement, while non-linear-elastic methods such as ultrasonic and Barkhausen noise are subject to errors from preferred orientation, cold work, grain size, and the need for stress-free reference samples [N5-F3]. It also notes that line broadening methods require careful interpretation of microstresses and damage, and that the full stress tensor can be determined only with certain limitations [N5-F3]. The practical guide in N5 further explains that the strain is calculated assuming linear elastic distortion of the crystal lattice, and that this makes the methods sensitive to simplifying assumptions about the residual stress field and sample geometry [N5-F3]. This means that the measured residual stress profile can be influenced by the measurement technique itself, and the results should not be taken as a direct representation of the true residual stress state without careful interpretation [N5-F3][N5-R2].

Interpreting residual stress profiles in the context of machining and loading requires understanding how manufacturing processes generate residual stresses and how those stresses interact with the applied load. The N5 evidence emphasizes that residual stress measurements are crucial for understanding the cause of failure, and that successful machining, grinding, shot peening, or heat treatment may hinge on achieving the appropriate surface finish, dimensions, case depth, or hardness along with a residual stress distribution [N5-F3]. The N2 case study on machined components also shows that residual stresses are important for fatigue strength and that surface roughness and residual stresses both affect fatigue behavior [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In practice, a residual stress profile should therefore be interpreted not in isolation but in relation to the part’s geometry, forming history, and loading conditions, because the same residual stress field can have different consequences depending on whether the component is subjected to tension, compression, or cyclic loading [N5-F3][N2-F2].

Measurement uncertainty affects fatigue strength predictions because residual stress profiles are not perfect representations of the actual stress state. The N5 evidence explicitly says that the available methods may be classified into linear-elastic methods and non-linear-elastic methods, and that the latter are subject to error from preferred orientation, cold work, grain size, and the need for stress-free reference samples [N5-F3]. The SPIF case study in N2 illustrates that fatigue lifetime and crack initiation must be predicted using residual stresses created in the forming process, validated by XRD measurements, and fitted to S–N curves [N2-F2]. This shows that uncertainty in residual stress measurement can propagate into the fatigue prediction chain, because the residual stress profile is used as input to fatigue analysis and affects the predicted fatigue life and crack initiation behavior [N2-F2]. The broader fatigue literature also suggests that the redistribution of residual stress due to crack propagation and the influence of crack closure make simple superposition inadequate, which further increases the sensitivity of predictions to the quality of the measured residual stress field [N1-F1].

Overall, residual stresses are best measured by XRD, neutron diffraction, and synchrotron diffraction, but each method has limitations related to assumptions, sample geometry, and measurement depth [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5]. Interpretation should connect the measured profile to the machining and loading context, and measurement uncertainty can significantly affect fatigue strength predictions because residual stress input is often used to calculate effective stress states and crack growth behavior [N5-F3][N2-F2].

Practical examples and engineering implications show that residual stress effects on load and fatigue are not uniform across components, loading conditions, and materials. The N6 evidence provides a direct case study of shot-peening residual stresses in an additively manufactured Co-Cr-Mo sample, where shot peening affected fatigue properties [N6-R3]. It also includes an example of shot peening and aging treatments on residual stresses and fatigue, showing that residual stress is a practical engineering issue with measurable effects on fatigue life [N6-R2]. The same N6 source states that shot peening can introduce residual compressive stresses on the surface of the part, and that in practical engineering most fatigue cracks occur from the surface [N6-R4]. This is important because it indicates that surface treatments can be directly relevant to fatigue failure, but their benefit depends on the part’s surface condition and the presence of defects.

The N2 evidence adds a broader engineering context: in incrementally formed sheet parts, residual stresses are important for fatigue strength, and the study used FE-Safe software to predict fatigue lifetime and crack initiation with numerically determined residual stresses validated by XRD [N2-F2]. This example shows that residual stress effects are not limited to simple shot-peened parts but are also relevant in complex formed components where residual stresses are created by forming processes [N2-F2]. The SPIF example also demonstrates that localized deformation can produce high strains and residual stresses, and that the resulting residual stress field is important for fatigue prediction [N2-F2]. This means that residual stress effects differ across loading conditions because the same forming process can produce different residual stress profiles depending on the forming path and strain distribution [N2-F2].

Across materials and loading conditions, residual stress effects can vary significantly. The N6 evidence explicitly notes that shot-peening residual stresses may have a detrimental effect in some cases when the largest defects are present, showing that residual stress benefits are not guaranteed and depend on defect state [N6-R1]. The N1 evidence also shows that crack propagation is influenced by the stress state, and that superposition methods are limited because they do not account for redistribution of residual stress and crack-generated residual stress [N1-F1]. This suggests that the engineering implications differ between materials and loading conditions because the way residual stresses interact with cyclic loading depends on the material’s response to plasticity, crack closure, and mean stress [N1-F1]. For example, compressive residual stresses may be more effective in high-strength materials where crack closure is strong, while tensile residual stresses may be more damaging in parts with surface defects [N2-F2][N6-R1].

Engineering decisions supported by residual stress analysis include choosing surface treatments, optimizing forming processes, and interpreting failure causes. The N5 evidence states that residual stress measurements are crucial for understanding the cause of failure and that successful machining, grinding, shot peening, or heat treatment may hinge on achieving the appropriate surface finish, dimensions, case depth, or hardness along with a residual stress distribution [N5-F3]. The N2 case study shows that residual stress profiles can be used to fit S–N curves and predict fatigue lifetime, supporting decisions about component design and process optimization [N2-F2]. The N6 example also supports decisions about shot peening and aging treatments because it links residual stress state to fatigue life and defect behavior [N6-R2][N6-R1]. In practice, residual stress analysis therefore supports decisions about whether a part should be shot peened, how forming should be designed, and whether failure is caused by residual stress, surface defects, or both [N5-F3][N2-F2][N6-R1].

In conclusion, practical examples show that residual stress effects on load and fatigue are material- and condition-dependent. Shot peening can improve fatigue strength by introducing compressive residual stresses, but its benefit can be reduced or even detrimental if defects are present [N6-R1][N6-R4]. Forming processes can also generate residual stresses that affect fatigue lifetime and crack initiation [N2-F2]. Residual stress analysis supports engineering decisions about treatment selection, forming optimization, and failure interpretation, because it connects the manufactured residual stress field to the applied load and fatigue behavior [N5-F3][N2-F2].

## Integrated explanation: How surface residual stresses interact with external cyclic stresses to affect load and fatigue strength

Surface residual stresses do not simply add to or subtract from external cyclic stresses in a fixed linear way. Instead, they modify the local stress state at the surface, influence crack behavior, and change how the component responds to cyclic loading. This interaction is central to fatigue strength because the combination of residual stress and applied load determines the effective stress range available for crack initiation and propagation [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The evidence shows that compressive residual stresses can delay crack initiation and improve fatigue life, while tensile residual stresses can promote premature failure [N2-R1][N2-F2][N6-R1].

### 1) Residual stresses modify the total stress state and do not act as simple additive/subtractive stresses

The evidence indicates that residual stresses interact with external cyclic stresses by altering the total stress state, not by simply adding or subtracting from it. Superposition methods are commonly used to assess residual stress effects, but they are limited because they assume an initial residual stress field and do not account for redistribution as a crack propagates [N1-F1]. In other words, residual stresses can be modified by crack growth and local plasticity, so their interaction with the applied load is dynamic rather than static [N1-F1]. This is important because the same external cyclic stress can behave differently depending on whether it is combined with compressive or tensile residual stress [N1-F1].

The stress state parameters mean stress and load ratio also matter because they control how the combined stress field affects fatigue life. The N1 evidence explains that the stress intensity factor range ΔK is independent of residual stress, while the stress ratio R is affected [N1-F1]. The mean stress correction literature adds that mean stress correction is used to account for non-zero mean stresses, and that the effect depends on material, stress state, environment, and strain amplitude [N4-R2]. Together, these sources show that residual stresses and external cyclic stresses jointly define the effective stress state, and the stress ratio R is especially important for fatigue prediction [N1-F1][N4-R2].

### 2) Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and reduce crack propagation

Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and affect crack propagation by counteracting elastic stress concentrations and increasing crack closure. The evidence says that compressive residual stress can counterbalance the elastic stress concentration generated by features such as FOD notches when external cyclic load is applied [N1-R2]. It also states that crack closure-based methodology gives better predictions than conventional superposition because crack closure reduces the effective ΔKeff and thus the crack growth rate [N1-F1]. This means that compressive residual stresses do not simply reduce the applied load; they change the local stress state in a way that makes crack initiation harder and crack propagation slower.

The broader fatigue evidence supports this: higher compressive residual stress induces longer fatigue life, and the influence of residual stresses on fatigue behavior can outperform that of surface roughness [N2-R1]. The SPIF case study further shows that compressive residual stresses and high tensile strength together determine resistance against crack initiation and fatigue life [N2-F2]. Taken together, these findings show that compressive residual stresses are beneficial because they delay crack initiation and reduce the effective driving force for crack growth [N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2].

### 3) Residual stress redistribution changes crack initiation and propagation

Residual stress redistribution is a key limitation of simple superposition methods. The evidence says that redistribution of residual stress due to crack propagation is a major reason why linear elastic superposition techniques can be nonconservative [N1-F1]. It also notes that crack closure and crack-generated residual stress are important in fatigue crack propagation, meaning that the residual stress field is not static once a crack begins to grow [N1-F1]. This implies that crack initiation and propagation are not only affected by the initial residual stress state, but also by how that state evolves as the crack advances.

This has important implications for fatigue strength. The N2 evidence shows that residual stresses are an important influencing factor for fatigue strength, and that crack initiation and fatigue life depend on residual stresses [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence further explains that fatigue crack growth is predicted using da/dN = f(ΔK, R), and that superposition methods are criticized for ignoring redistribution of residual stress and crack-generated residual stress [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that residual stress redistribution can change the effective stress intensity range and crack growth behavior, making the fatigue response more sensitive to local conditions than a simple superposition approach would suggest [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 4) Residual stresses alter the fatigue limit and S–N curve shape

Residual stresses alter the fatigue limit and change the shape of the S–N curve because they shift the relationship between alternating stress magnitude and cycles to failure. The evidence shows that higher compressive residual stress induces longer fatigue life and that the influence of residual stresses on fatigue behavior can outperform that of surface roughness [N2-R1]. The SPIF case study explicitly states that fatigue strength is crucial for metals and their alloys, and that compressive residual stresses and high tensile strength together determine resistance against crack initiation and fatigue life [N2-F2]. It also says that residual stresses are an important influencing factor for fatigue strength [N2-F2].

This directly supports the idea that residual stresses shift the fatigue limit and change the S–N curve shape. The case study also shows that fatigue lifetime and crack initiation were predicted using S–N curves fitted from experimental fatigue testing, with residual stresses validated by XRD measurements [N2-F2]. This means that residual stresses can raise the fatigue limit by reducing the effective stress range that drives crack initiation and growth, and that the S–N curve can shift upward or change its slope depending on whether residual stresses are compressive or tensile [N2-R1][N2-F2].

### 5) Surface treatments like shot peening improve fatigue strength by generating compressive residual stresses

Surface treatments such as shot peening improve fatigue strength by generating beneficial compressive residual stresses. The evidence in N3 says shot peening is an efficient technique to improve fatigue behavior of metal components, and that each shot strike creates a dimple and beneficial compressive residual stress [N3-R2]. It also states that shot peening can have potentially positive effects on residual compressive stress, work hardening, surface roughness, and other factors [N3-R3]. The N6 evidence adds that shot peening can introduce residual compressive stresses on the surface of the part, and that most fatigue cracks in engineering practice occur from the surface [N6-R4]. This is especially relevant because surface treatments are often used to modify the residual stress field at the location where fatigue cracks typically initiate.

However, the evidence also shows that the benefit is not always guaranteed. The N6 example states that shot-peening residual stresses may have a detrimental effect in some cases when the largest defects are present [N6-R1]. This highlights that surface treatments can improve fatigue strength, but their effectiveness depends on the local defect state, geometry, and loading conditions [N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### 6) Measurement, interpretation, and uncertainty affect fatigue predictions

Residual stresses are measured using several common methods, each with distinct strengths and limitations. The evidence identifies X-ray diffraction (XRD), neutron diffraction, and synchrotron diffraction as key methods [N5-F3][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. XRD is described as a nondestructive method for measuring residual stress in fine-grained crystalline materials, while neutron diffraction is used for bulk residual stress data in thick sections [N5-F3][N5-R1]. Synchrotron diffraction allows measurement at arbitrary depth and improves spatial resolution [N5-R5].

The main limitations include assumptions about the residual stress field, sample geometry, and linear elasticity. The evidence notes that mechanical methods are necessarily destructive, while non-linear-elastic methods such as ultrasonic and Barkhausen noise are subject to errors from preferred orientation, cold work, grain size, and the need for stress-free reference samples [N5-F3]. It also states that line broadening methods require careful interpretation of microstresses and damage, and that the full stress tensor can be determined only with certain limitations [N5-F3]. This means that residual stress profiles should not be taken as a direct representation of the true stress state without careful interpretation [N5-F3].

Instead, they modify the local stress state at the surface, influence crack behavior, and change how the component responds to cyclic loading. The evidence shows that compressive residual stresses can delay crack initiation and improve fatigue life, while tensile residual stresses can promote premature failure [N2-R1][N2-F2][N6-R1].

### 1) Residual stresses modify the total stress state and do not act as simple additive/subtractive stresses

The evidence indicates that residual stresses interact with external cyclic stresses by altering the total stress state, not by simply adding or subtracting from it. Superposition methods are commonly used to assess residual stress effects, but they are limited because they assume an initial residual stress field and do not account for redistribution as a crack propagates [N1-F1]. In other words, residual stresses can be modified by crack growth and local plasticity, so their interaction with the applied load is dynamic rather than static [N1-F1]. This is important because the same external cyclic stress can behave differently depending on whether it is combined with compressive or tensile residual stress [N1-F1].

The stress state parameters mean stress and load ratio also matter because they control how the combined stress field affects fatigue life. The N1 evidence explains that the stress intensity factor range ΔK is independent of residual stress, while the stress ratio R is affected [N1-F1]. The mean stress correction literature adds that mean stress correction is used to account for non-zero mean stresses, and that the effect depends on material, stress state, environment, and strain amplitude [N4-R2]. Together, these sources show that residual stresses and external cyclic stresses jointly define the effective stress state, and the stress ratio R is especially important for fatigue prediction [N1-F1][N4-R2].

### 2) Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and reduce crack propagation

Compressive residual stresses delay crack initiation and affect crack propagation by counteracting elastic stress concentrations and increasing crack closure. The evidence says that compressive residual stress can counterbalance the elastic stress concentration generated by features such as FOD notches when external cyclic load is applied [N1-R2]. It also states that crack closure-based methodology gives better predictions than conventional superposition because crack closure reduces the effective ΔKeff and thus the crack growth rate [N1-F1]. This means that compressive residual stresses do not simply reduce the applied load; they change the local stress state in a way that makes crack initiation harder and crack propagation slower.

The broader fatigue evidence supports this: higher compressive residual stress induces longer fatigue life, and the influence of residual stresses on fatigue behavior can outperform that of surface roughness [N2-R1]. The SPIF case study further shows that compressive residual stresses and high tensile strength together determine resistance against crack initiation and fatigue life [N2-F2]. Taken together, these findings show that compressive residual stresses are beneficial because they delay crack initiation and reduce the effective driving force for crack growth [N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2].

### 3) Residual stress redistribution changes crack initiation and propagation

Residual stress redistribution is a key limitation of simple superposition methods. The evidence says that redistribution of residual stress due to crack propagation is a major reason why linear elastic superposition techniques can be nonconservative [N1-F1]. It also notes that crack closure and crack-generated residual stress are important in fatigue crack propagation, meaning that the residual stress field is not static once a crack begins to grow [N1-F1]. This implies that crack initiation and propagation are not only affected by the initial residual stress state, but also by how that state evolves as the crack advances.

This has important implications for fatigue strength. The N2 evidence shows that residual stresses are an important influencing factor for fatigue strength, and that crack initiation and fatigue life depend on residual stresses [N2-F2]. The N1 evidence further explains that fatigue crack growth is predicted using da/dN = f(ΔK, R), and that superposition methods are criticized for ignoring redistribution of residual stress and crack-generated residual stress [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that residual stress redistribution can change the effective stress intensity range and crack growth behavior, making the fatigue response more sensitive to local conditions than a simple superposition approach would suggest [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Residual stresses alter the fatigue limit and change the shape of the S–N curve because they shift the relationship between alternating stress magnitude and cycles to failure. The SPIF case study explicitly states that fatigue strength is crucial for metals and their alloys, and that compressive residual stresses and high tensile strength together determine resistance against crack initiation and fatigue life [N2-F2]. ## Bottom line

Surface residual stresses interact with external cyclic stresses by modifying the total stress state at the surface, influencing crack behavior, and changing the effective stress range available for crack initiation and propagation.
